falas.txt: This laser just hit a droplet of molten tin, thinner than a human hair, flying at two hundred and fifty kilometers an hour.

v.k: A droplet thinner than a hair, at *250 km/h*.

falas.txt: Then it hit the same droplet again.

v.k: Then it hit it *again*.

falas.txt: It does that fifty thousand times a second. All day. For years.
Every advanced AI chip on Earth starts with that flash of light.
The machine that uses it is built by A-S-M-L. The laser is not.
A-S-M-L buys it from one family owned company in southern Germany.

v.l2: The laser: one family company in Germany.

falas.txt: On paper, it doesn't sound hard. You need a laser.
A powerful one. About forty kilowatts.
And a droplet of tin to aim it at.
Lasers that powerful have cut steel in factories for decades.

v.k: Lasers this powerful have *cut steel for decades*.

falas.txt: And yet there is no second supplier. Anywhere.
So why can't anyone copy a laser?

v.sub: Why can't anyone copy a laser?

falas.txt: There are five locks.

nomes: A speck of tin at 250 km/h
Hit it twice, 50,000 times a second

falas.txt: Four are physics and engineering.
The fifth is about who would ever pay you to try.
And it's the one no engineer can fix.

v.k: The one *no engineer* can fix.

falas.txt: Lock one. The target.

fonte: ASML (HOW EUV LIGHT IS MADE) · LASER FOCUS WORLD

falas.txt: Inside the machine, there's a vacuum chamber.

tit: The target: a speck of tin, *already gone*.

falas.txt: A nozzle fires a stream of molten tin droplets across it.
Each droplet is about thirty thousandths of a millimeter wide. Less than half a human hair.
They leave the nozzle at seventy meters per second. That's two hundred and fifty kilometers an hour.
And there are fifty thousand of them, every second.
Your laser has to find each one, in flight, and hit it dead center.

v.k: Find each one, in flight. Hit it *dead center*.

falas.txt: Miss by a hair, literally, and that droplet makes no light at all.

v.k: Miss by a hair, and you get *no light*.

falas.txt: Lock two. The two shots.
Here's the problem. A round droplet is a terrible target.

tit: One shot shapes it. *The next one* burns it.

falas.txt: It's tiny, and most of the laser beam would fly right past it.
So the laser shoots twice.

v.k: So the laser shoots *twice*.

falas.txt: The first shot is weak. It's called the pre pulse. It doesn't destroy the droplet. It flattens it, into a thin disc, like a pancake.
Now the target is wide, and thin.
A split second later, the main pulse arrives, and turns that pancake into a plasma, hotter than the surface of the Sun.
That plasma gives off the light that prints the chip.
Two shots per droplet. Fifty thousand droplets a second.
That's a hundred thousand hits, every second.
And the second shot has to land on a target that the first shot just changed.

v.k: Shot two hits a target that shot one *just changed*.

falas.txt: If the timing between them drifts, the pancake is the wrong shape, and the light fades.

v.k: Wrong timing, wrong shape, *less light*.

falas.txt: Lock three. The power.
The pulse doesn't start out powerful.

tit: From a few watts to *40 kilowatts*.

falas.txt: It begins in a small seed laser, at just a few watts. About as much as a phone charger.
That's on purpose. A weak pulse is easy to shape precisely.

v.k: A weak pulse is *easy to shape*.

falas.txt: Then it goes through a chain of amplifiers, one after another.
Each one adds energy, without ruining the shape.
By the end, the pulse has been amplified more than ten thousand times.
Up to forty kilowatts of average power. With peaks in the millions of watts.
The company that builds it calls it the most powerful pulsed industrial laser in the world.

v.k: The most powerful pulsed industrial laser *in the world*.

fonte: TRUMPF ("FLASHES OF LIGHT IN A VACUUM") · LASER FOCUS WORLD

falas.txt: And here's the painful part. Almost all of that power is wasted.
Tens of thousands of watts of laser go in. A few hundred watts of usable light come out.
Only a few percent of the energy becomes the light you actually want.

v.k: Only *a few percent* becomes useful light.

falas.txt: So you can't build a smaller, easier laser. You need all of it, just to get that little.

v.k: You can't build a smaller one. You need *all of it*.

falas.txt: Quick question, before the next lock.
You fire the most powerful laser of its kind at a tiny ball of liquid metal. What do you think the metal does to the laser?
Put your guess in the comments. The answer is lock four.
Lock four. The echo.
The laser isn't even in the same room as the droplet.
It sits on the floor below, in the basement of the chip factory.
The beam travels up through a transport system that can be thirty meters long, and is focused onto the droplet at the very end.
Now remember what the droplet is. Liquid metal. And metal is a mirror.

v.k: Liquid metal is *a mirror*.

falas.txt: So part of that enormous pulse bounces straight back, down the same path it came from.
Back toward amplifiers that are built to make any light passing through them stronger.
Without protection, the laser would amplify its own reflection, and aim it at its most delicate part. The seed.

v.k: It would amplify *its own echo*, and aim it at the seed.

falas.txt: So the machine is full of defenses. Guards against reflections. Three separate cooling circuits. Optics that have to stay perfectly clean.
One laser amplifier has four hundred and fifty seven thousand, three hundred and twenty nine parts.
More than seven kilometers of cable.
And it weighs seventeen tons.
That's not a laser. That's a building's worth of machine, with one job. Hit the droplet. Twice.

v.k: One job: *hit the droplet. Twice.*

falas.txt: That's four locks.

nomes: A speck of tin at 250 km/h
Hit it twice, 50,000 times a second

falas.txt: A target smaller than a hair.
Two shots, a hundred thousand times a second.
Forty kilowatts, built up from almost nothing.
And an echo that tries to destroy the laser.
All four are solvable. There are brilliant laser companies in America, Japan and China.

v.k: There are brilliant laser companies everywhere.

falas.txt: So why hasn't one of them built a second one?

v.k: So why hasn't anyone built *a second one*?

falas.txt: The fifth lock.

nomes: A speck of tin at 250 km/h
Hit it twice, 50,000 times a second

falas.txt: It has nothing to do with lasers.

v.k: It has *nothing to do* with lasers.

falas.txt: Lock five.
The company that builds this laser is called TRUMPF. It was founded in nineteen twenty three, near Stuttgart.

v.sub: Founded in 1923. Still owned by one family.

falas.txt: And it isn't really a chip company at all.
Most of its money comes from machines that cut and bend sheet metal.

v.cab: TRUMPF SALES BY BUSINESS, FISCAL 2025/26, € BILLION

falas.txt: Then industrial lasers.
The lasers for chip machines are the smallest of the three. Seven hundred and ninety one million euros, out of more than four billion.
That's the secret. This laser was never invented for chips.

v.k: This laser was *never invented for chips*.

falas.txt: That's lock five. The day job.
TRUMPF spent decades building this kind of laser for a completely different reason. To cut steel in factories.

v.sub: Decades of building this laser, to cut steel.

falas.txt: Thousands of machines. Thousands of customers. Every one of them paid for a little more experience.

v.sub: Thousands of machines paid for the experience.

falas.txt: By the time the chip industry needed an impossible laser, one company had already been paid to learn how.

v.sub: One company had already been paid to learn how.

falas.txt: Now look at it from a copycat's side.

la: No steel cutting business to learn from
That customer already has a supplier
lb: The one customer is a partner
Owned by a family, not for sale

falas.txt: You'd have no day job to learn from. Much of the cutting industry has since moved on to a newer kind of laser.
You'd have exactly one possible customer on Earth. A-S-M-L.
And that customer already has a supplier it has worked with for years.
And even for the original, one customer is a dangerous thing.
In a single year, when A-S-M-L ordered fewer machines, TRUMPF's laser sales to it fell twenty three percent.
They've only partly recovered.
So who spends ten years and billions of dollars, to become the backup supplier to a single customer?

v.k: Who spends billions to be *the backup* for one customer?

falas.txt: And you can't buy your way in, either.
TRUMPF isn't on the stock market. Ninety percent belongs to one family. The other ten, to the family's foundation.
So here's what a real copy would need.

it: A CUSTOMER THAT NEEDS A SECOND ONE
v.cab: WHAT A REAL COPY WOULD NEED

falas.txt: A laser that hits twice.
Forty kilowatts that survive their own echo.
Decades of a day job that taught you how.
And a customer that actually needs a second supplier.
You can copy the laser.
You can't copy the reason it exists.

v.l2: You can't copy the reason it exists.

falas.txt: If you know someone who thinks the chip race is only about chips, send them this video.
Because it's about to get harder.

fonte: ASML (1,000 W SOURCE ROADMAP), VIA HEISE AND TOM'S HARDWARE

falas.txt: One last thing.
A-S-M-L wants its machines to print about fifty percent more wafers by twenty thirty.

it: THE EUV LIGHT SOURCE IT NEEDS

falas.txt: To do that, the light source has to reach a thousand watts.
The plan for getting there is public. Twice as many droplets. And three laser pulses on each one, instead of two.
The target is about to get twice as fast.

v.k: The target is about to get *twice as fast*.

falas.txt: So that's the real reason nobody can copy this laser.

v.k: The real reason nobody can copy this laser:

falas.txt: By the time you learn to hit the droplet twice, the original is already hitting it three times.

v.k: Learn to hit it twice, and the original is *hitting it three times*.

falas.txt: The laser is one link in a chain. And almost every link has a company like this hiding in it.
Next, we open another one.
